# Facade repeated-close trial record

This review put the two entry points in the same record, but did not treat them as the same problem. CAP-205 is for existing tests or examples to trigger a facade close, with emphasis on branches not yet covered by the user path; CAP-222 requires the zero-copy finalizing buffer lifetime to be exercised through routine calls, while retaining the return value or raw diagnostic. The former checks when the object is no longer usable; the latter checks when use of the already-handed-out pixel view ends.

At the start, we considered looking for common clues in Linux type declarations. The Display, XErrorEvent, XFixesCursorImage, XImage, XRRCrtcInfo, XRRModeInfo, and XRRScreenResources in `src/mss/linux.py` are useful for locating the review on the X11 object side; they do not establish the close count between the facade and the selected implementation. The record therefore narrowed its focus to two points: how many times implementation cleanup occurs, and the result of the second close call.

## Review setup

The operation sequence stayed minimal: first obtain a capture facade for a selected implementation, call close once, then, without switching implementations or obtaining another facade, call close a second time. Pixel content is not a criterion here; whether cleanup repeats and whether the second call fails are the results to record. Zero-copy conversion was not included in this round's assertions because its interruption point and the facade's resource boundary are different.

The interface contract after the review is:

> Closing a capture facade twice is safe: the first close releases its selected implementation, while later close calls neither invoke implementation cleanup again nor fail because the facade is already closed.

This puts the checkpoint on the facade itself, rather than requiring every implementation to accept arbitrary repeated cleanup. The first close still releases the implementation selected at that point; the second close only needs to leave the facade in the closed state and should not send another cleanup request into the implementation. If the record shows the second call reaching the implementation side, first check the closed state stored by the facade, then inspect the specific backend.

CAP-222 remains separate. It verifies the buffer lifetime after the view finalizer is established and the conversion is interrupted; there is currently no evidence that this reclamation timing should be attributed to the second close. Next time, change only the conversion entry point: use the routine call rather than the debug entry point, retain the return value or raw diagnostic, and compare it side by side with the consecutive-close results on this page.

# Capture Bounds and Writable Views Decision

In the compatibility work for Aperture 11, tuple capture bounds and pixel results were discussed as part of the same screenshot path, but they should not be handled by the same layer.

The tentative decision is to interpret caller-supplied tuple capture bounds before delegating to a specific capture strategy. The strategy receives a region ready for capture and should not reinterpret tuple field positions or coordinate semantics in its own branch.

Pixel results are handled separately. Results exposed to callers need to retain writable ctypes-compatible pixel views; this is not part of the region object, and "being able to read the screenshot" is not a substitute. Callers also need to be able to keep writing to the views and interface with ctypes.

We did not adopt the combination of "each backend interprets tuples itself, and the result object exports copies on demand." It scatters region semantics across strategies and makes view capabilities vary with the result path.

It is not yet confirmed whether all existing tuple entry points reach delegation through the same layer; this draft also leaves open how views are retained after conversion.

# Capture Bounds and Writable View Decision

The initial draft compressed the compatibility work into one sentence: "Handle tuple near the screenshot entry point and retain writable views." After review, this sentence can no longer serve as the wording of the decision. It conflates two adjacent issues into one change package: one is where a request becomes a capture region, and the other is how the pixels can still be used after they are returned.

`src/mss/windows.py` is one of the paths checked during this review. The file header's `ctypes`, `sys`, along with `POINTER`, `WINFUNCTYPE`, `Structure`, `c_int`, and `c_void_p`, show that this location directly handles Windows native interfaces and structure definitions. Earlier notes therefore also attributed region interpretation to this location. That attribution went too far: being adjacent to the path and native pixel delivery does not mean it owns the region semantics of every capture entry point. This correction is retained in the document to prevent a later Windows-side check from being mistaken for complete closure.

## Decisions Made

The first decision is **tuple capture bounds before delegation**. Here, before refers to the delegation boundary, not a performance recommendation. The tuple passed by the caller must first undergo the required bounds interpretation and only then be handed to the selected capture strategy. This ensures that a strategy does not change the roles of the same tuple fields based on its implementation, and does not need to add another coordinate interpretation inside the branch.

The second decision is to retain **writable ctypes-compatible pixel views**. This is a result-delivery requirement, not an ancillary action of the first decision. After receiving the pixels, the caller must still be able to write to them and continue using them as ctypes-compatible views; the result cannot be considered compliant merely because the screenshot content is readable.

Both decisions came from the same round of compatibility work, so they are easy to implement together; their responsibility boundaries are nevertheless different. The first answers "Whether the region has been fully determined before the strategy starts working"; the second answers "What the object received by the caller can still do when the pixels leave the capture path." Separating the two means that when investigating screenshot anomalies, we at least do not have to first alternate guesses between region interpretation and buffer capabilities.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> TupleInput
    TupleInput: tuple capture bounds
    TupleInput --> BoundsReady
    BoundsReady: bounds interpreted
    BoundsReady --> StrategyDelegation
    StrategyDelegation: delegated to capture strategy
    StrategyDelegation --> PixelResult
    PixelResult: pixel result
    PixelResult --> WritableView
    WritableView: writable ctypes-compatible pixel views
```

The sequence in the diagram describes only the interface boundaries required by this decision. It does not specify how the strategy obtains pixels or whether intermediate objects exist internally. The Windows path may have its own native calls and structure handling; the capture facade, strategy selection point, and result object still need to be checked separately.

## Arrangements Considered at the Time

| Arrangement | Reason Not Adopted |
| --- | --- |
| Have each strategy directly receive and interpret the tuple | The interpretation point for the same call shape would change with the strategy branch, making it difficult for the caller to have stable expectations about region semantics. |
| Add a unified interpretation layer after selecting the strategy | Although the common logic would still exist, the strategy entry point would already have received an undetermined input; this would not satisfy the requirement to determine it before delegation. |
| Deliver only a byte copy that is convenient to read | Being readable does not mean being writable, and does not guarantee continued ctypes compatibility. |
| Retain a separate writable buffer at each conversion entry point | Buffer capabilities would follow the conversion entry point, making compatibility an accidental result. |

The appeal of the first option is that it requires only a small local change. Each strategy was already handling capture, so continuing to accept the raw tuple appears to be the easiest approach. But it makes "which branch interprets the region" part of the caller's behavior. When strategies are added or replaced later, the region semantics will move with the implementation. What must be fixed here is the boundary before the strategy receives the input, not making every backend's internal implementation take the same shape.

The second option is more like a patch to the first: complete strategy selection first, then organize the tuple at some point. It still leaves an unnecessary state in which the specific strategy has already been selected but has not yet received a region that can be captured directly. This state makes verification ambiguous: when the screenshot result is wrong, it is impossible to first determine whether the problem is in the strategy itself or whether the region interpretation added after selection introduced the discrepancy. It was therefore not adopted.

There is similar misdirection on the pixel-view side. If we check only whether "the screenshot is returned," the differences between read-only, copied, and writable results will all be hidden. In particular, a conversion path can easily preserve the pixel content while changing the caller's ability to continue using the buffer. The initial draft's wording about "avoiding extra copies where possible" was only a preference during selection, not the decision itself. The existence of an internal copy cannot independently be judged wrong; the view delivered to the caller must still be writable ctypes-compatible pixel views to satisfy this requirement.

## Two Changes to the Previous Draft's Wording

The previous draft said that the tuple should be handled "near the entry point." That wording is too broad and even allows the region to be carried all the way into the strategy branch before being interpreted. It is now changed to "handle before delegation." During review, there is no need to first ask whether each strategy can eventually take a screenshot; instead, first identify whether the tuple has completed its required bounds interpretation before the strategy starts taking responsibility for the work.

The previous draft also described the pixel view as a buffer detail on the Windows path. The ctypes adjacency of `src/mss/windows.py` does make it a suitable entry point for review, but the requirement that the view be writable and ctypes-compatible belongs to result delivery. If the same result object behaves differently through different conversion entry points, the issue should not be described as "the Windows screenshot succeeded but happened to be inconvenient to use elsewhere"; it should be treated directly as inconsistent result capabilities.

This does not exclude the Windows file from the implementation. On the contrary, `ctypes` and the related structure declarations make it worth checking pixel-data handling near the native interface first. What is rejected here is another form of overreach: the fact that the file appears in the path alone cannot justify pushing all tuple rules into that file or reducing the entire buffer contract to one native call.

## Separate Tracks for Follow-up Verification

CAP-206 is used to locate call sites that still use tuple capture bounds before delegation. After responsibility was confirmed, this card still had a record of "one unconfirmed location," and it subsequently entered the in-progress state. This gap should continue to be checked by entry point, actual version, and current result; it should not be taken as evidence that the bounds decision has failed. The decision has already specified where interpretation occurs; what remains unconfirmed is whether a particular existing entry point actually follows that location.

The goal of CAP-223 is different: to inventory the current dependents of writable ctypes-compatible pixel views. The card explicitly leaves evidence-free areas blank, so the entry-point status in CAP-206 cannot be used in place of a pixel-view conclusion, nor can a single Windows path check replace the dependent list. The two cards serve region boundaries and result capabilities separately, and their counts must not be merged in the records.

DOC-16 retains structured Windows API failure information, along with discussion of Pillow and the NumPy conversion layout. These items may be adjacent to the result object, but they do not change the tradeoff on this page. In particular, a convenient conversion layout cannot be used to work backward and decide where the tuple should be interpreted; likewise, the fact that the tuple was handled early cannot be treated as evidence that a particular pixel layout is already established.

For now, understand it as follows: before a capture request enters the strategy, tuple capture bounds have been interpreted; the strategy receives a region that can be captured. Result delivery retains writable ctypes-compatible pixel views, and successful screenshots or readable pixels cannot substitute for this requirement.

Still to be filled in are the entry point referred to by CAP-206, and the dependents not yet recorded in the CAP-223 inventory. The former requires checking the actual entry point and result; the latter requires adding observations of views in actual use. These items affect verification coverage but do not change the two decisions made on this page.

# Windows Error and Conversion Layout Proposal

For this round of interface review, first record two potentially related gaps: whether the exception a caller receives when a Windows call fails is enough to identify the point of failure; and whether the caller can know the pixel order and array layout in advance when converting an image object for Pillow or NumPy.

The initial investigation focused on `src/mss/linux.py`. The file contains ctypes structures including `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, and `XImage`; the idea at the time was to use these declarations as a starting point for a unified error and pixel description layer. This idea is still only a starting point; it should not be taken to mean that the Linux structures will directly determine the Windows-side exception objects.

Tentative approach:

- Preserve the underlying call name and original arguments on Windows failure paths, rather than returning only a formatted error message;
- Set one explicit image mode for Pillow conversion first, then discuss whether callers should be allowed to pass in other modes;
- NumPy conversion should not rely on callers guessing dimensions; the layout name should be provided with the interface.

Record the conditions for dropping this approach as well: if preserving call arguments would expose objects that do not belong in an exception, or if the two conversion entry points cannot share the same pixel interpretation, do not force them together just for superficial consistency. # Windows Errors and Conversion Layout Proposal

This interface review still centers on two questions: what to retain when a Windows call fails, and how to describe the layout when the same screenshot data is passed to Pillow and NumPy. Early notes treated `src/mss/linux.py` as the main entry point; ctypes declarations such as `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, and `XImage` are visible there. It is useful for looking up old structure definitions, but does not establish that those structures should serve as a shared container for Windows exception details or conversion interfaces.

## Earlier Assessment Retained

The initial preference was to put "error descriptions" and "pixel descriptions" into a shared object layer, since callers do not want to keep guessing at internal state in either case. That assessment has been retained: it explains why the first draft put both topics on the same page. But on review, a shared wrapper does not imply shared fields. Error details provide information on the failure path, while pixel layout explains a successful return value. Tying them together just because their names are similar would conflate exception compatibility and image compatibility in subsequent changes.

## Review Addendum

The routine checklist for CAP-207 calls for evidence of structured Windows API failure details; missing portions remain blank. CAP-224 stems from inconsistent results reported by Pillow users and calls for adding the most recent actual invocation and the result the user saw. Looking at the two cards together, the original sequence of "define a shared description layer first, then add samples" is not appropriate. We first need to establish which information callers can reliably read from exceptions, then check whether the conversion entry points really have the same input and output boundary.

The recommendation is to separate out a candidate details bundle for the Windows side. For a failed `ScreenShotError`, we could retain the name of the failed function, the original arguments, and the text returned by the system. Whether these fields become a stable public interface should be decided after checking samples from existing callers. This would be easier to investigate than a single concatenated error message, while keeping platform-specific content out of normal screenshot objects.

On the conversion side, do not commit yet to a single parameter set for Pillow and NumPy. Pillow needs an image mode; NumPy needs an array layout. Both start from a pixel buffer, but their invocation and error handling may differ. Each entry point can first state which modes or layouts it accepts and document how unsupported values fail. The invocation samples for CAP-224 have not yet been added back, so this part cannot be treated as an established compatibility conclusion.

## Open Questions

- Which arguments can be retained unchanged in exception details, and which need to be trimmed during construction?
- Do the inconsistent Pillow results arise from mode interpretation, channel selection, or subsequent processing by the caller?
- Would adding aliases for NumPy layouts cause existing callers to depend on an undeclared dimension order?

If the samples show that callers only need the error text, the details bundle should not be a release prerequisite. If the samples show that the two conversions interpret the buffer differently, withdraw the shared conversion options and retain only the documentation for each entry point.

# Windows Errors and Conversion Layout Proposal

This page records an interface proposal that was never fully closed out. It was later still cited by CAP-207 and CAP-224, but it must not be treated as the latest implementation documentation: the early tradeoffs, the call samples that were missing at the time, and an attempt at unification that has since been scaled back are all retained below.

## Drafting Starting Point (Retained)

The initial draft started from `src/mss/linux.py`. That file directly contains the definitions of `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, `XImage`, `XRRCrtcInfo`, `XRRModeInfo`, and `XRRScreenResources`, while its header also includes dependencies on `ctypes`, `os`, and `suppress`. At the time, these declarations were treated as clues for a "unified error and pixel description layer": since the platform layer already had many structured objects, Windows failure details and image conversion might be conveniently grouped into the same description object.

This judgment is now retained only as historical context. It led the investigation to the right area of the repository, but placed two different compatibility surfaces too close together. The structure declarations in the Linux file can help review types and old local conventions; they cannot define the fields of the Windows API failure object, nor can they define the output layout for Pillow or NumPy.

## Later Review

CAP-207 was added as the inspection entry point for structured Windows API failure details, requiring checks to follow the maintainer's routine steps and forbidding unsupported conclusions where evidence is missing. CAP-224 records the inconsistent results seen by Pillow users and requires recovering the most recent real call and its result. These two items changed the proposal's order: the previously envisioned shared description layer lacked sufficient support, so the problem should first be split into failure information and successful-data paths.

There is one misunderstanding that has not been fully resolved. Early discussions attributed both "looking wrong after conversion" and "having no context after a capture call failed" to insufficient object descriptions. The former may occur in mode or layout interpretation, while the latter occurs during exception construction; even though both involve screenshot data, callers do not read them at the same time. No complete call sample that could be included on this page was found later, so we cannot claim in retrospect that both problems have been solved by the same interface.

## Candidate Boundary for Windows Failure Details

The recommendation is to retain a sufficiently small detail object rather than merely appending system text to the exception message. The candidate fields are `func`, `args`, and `error_msg`: the first points to the failed underlying call, the second stores the original argument tuple that triggered the call, and the last stores the underlying system error text. This allows the caller, after receiving `ScreenShotError`, to determine which call caused the failure and retain the original context for reproduction.

This does not require every failure point to include an arbitrary object. The early design tended to put all available information into the details; if the arguments contained handles or lifetime-bound objects that were unsuitable for long-term exposure, the exception details themselves would become a compatibility burden. The safer approach is to retain only these three categories of information—the call name, original arguments, and error text—and keep additional context inside the platform implementation.

Likewise, Windows' underlying error text should not be rewritten into another generic category merely to pursue format consistency. Callers need a locatable failure point and the original cause, not a seemingly tidy summary that loses its source. CAP-207 can continue to serve as the verification entry point; this page does not include samples sufficient to confirm every failure branch, so field names and null handling still need to follow the actual callers.

## Do Not Reuse the Exception Model for Conversion Entry Points

Pillow and NumPy share the source of the screenshot pixels, not the same user interface. Pillow output needs an explicit image mode; in the current proposal, `RGBA` is used as the pixel mode for this entry point. The dimensional interpretation of NumPy should instead be specified by the layout parameter, with `CHW` indicating channel-height-width ordering. Neither should allow the caller to infer the order solely from the buffer length.

The original design had one option that has since been scaled back: using the same "format parameter" to control both the Pillow mode and the NumPy layout. The benefit is fewer entry points; the drawback is that the semantics of a mode and of array axes are different. When the caller passes the wrong value, the resulting error also becomes difficult to interpret. The issue in CAP-224 is a reminder of this: inconsistent results seen by users may not originate in capture itself, but may instead result from treating an image mode as an array layout, or conversely using a layout name for image conversion.

Therefore, the direction is to retain two independent entry points. The Pillow parameter should address only allowed image modes; the NumPy parameter should address only allowed channels and layouts. For unsupported values, validation failure should be reported as `ValueError`, rather than silently rearranging the data. As for whether the two sides should share an internal buffer adapter layer, this old proposal does not contain enough material to decide; separating the interfaces does not automatically require duplicate internal implementations.

## Rollback Criteria Still Undecided

If later call samples show that fields beyond `func`, `args`, and `error_msg` must also be exposed consistently, the current small detail bundle must be reopened rather than temporarily adding ambiguously named keys in a compatibility release. Conversely, if callers consume only the error text, the detail fields can remain platform-side supplements and should not force changes to every exception path.

The rollback condition for the conversion portion is more direct: only if real calls show that Pillow and NumPy truly have exactly the same data interpretation should shared parameters be reevaluated; merging them merely because both come from the same `ScreenShot` has already been rejected by this review. The invocation methods and user-visible results required by CAP-224 have still not been written into this page and are left for the card record; this page retains only why the unified entry point was not pursued further at the time.

# XShm Cleanup and Region Construction Decision

## Branches Left by the Initial Draft

The earliest record was less than a page long: the Aperture 11 compatibility train contained both interrupted XShm conversion cleanup and the Region constructor normalization boundary. Both were grouped near Linux compatibility, so they initially looked like two sides of one change. That version entered through `src/mss/linux.py`, first showing the structure definitions and then placing exception cleanup and constructor-parameter organization on the same task list.

The initial draft did not provide actual output from successful or failed calls. It left only one judgment: if the conversion is interrupted after obtaining the image view, the release order needs to be checked separately; if the Region has already been normalized before entering the backend, the constructor may be a different boundary. This judgment was not treated as a completion criterion, and the file location of `src/mss/linux.py` was not written down as proof of the Region implementation.

## File Evidence and the First Decision

The objects that can be confirmed along this path are limited. Near the beginning there is `class Display(Structure):`, followed by `class XErrorEvent(Structure):`, `class XFixesCursorImage(Structure):`, and `class XImage(Structure):`; farther on, `XRRCrtcInfo`, `XRRModeInfo`, and `XRRScreenResources` can be seen as structures related to X11. The file header uses `from __future__ import annotations`, `import os`, and `from contextlib import suppress`, and imports a set of declaration utilities from `ctypes`.

This material supports one local decision: interrupted cleanup for the XShm conversion should continue to be traced through the Linux X11 materials, but Region construction normalization should not be automatically included just because it is in the same compatibility train. Another direction that was considered was to combine the two into one "compatibility cleanup," which would make the change look more concentrated, at the cost of making the failure behavior and the pre-construction state impossible to assess separately. This combined framing was not adopted.

There was also a more aggressive direction: infer the call chain solely from the structure names in the file, then work backward to determine which object owns the finalization action. There was not enough material for this direction during the initial-draft stage. The structure declarations identify objects that can be looked up, but they do not preserve the call order, resource ownership, or direct location of Region construction. Therefore, the record retains "a place to start investigating," but does not write "this is the complete set of entry points."

## The XShm Thread

The issue with interrupted XShm conversion cleanup is not to rewrite an exception as an ordinary failure. Two scenarios must be examined separately: when the conversion returns completely, the image result seen by the caller; and when the conversion is interrupted midway, whether the image-related state already obtained, the temporary view, and the shared resources still exist. The former can only show that the success path works; it cannot replace the latter.

The approaches compared early on can be summarized as three options. The first releases the resources already obtained immediately in the conversion function's exception branch. The code is short, but if the view or context is still used by later cleanup, the ordering can easily be obscured. The second registers the finalization action when the temporary image view is created, so normal return and exceptional exit go through the same release point. Its advantage is that the interruption point is easier to compare; the cost is that it must be confirmed that registration occurs early enough. The third delegates cleanup to the outer caller. The local function is simpler, but the caller must know the conversion process's internal state.

What the history actually retains is the second option as the more reliable working direction, not as an already-accepted implementation description. The reason is specific: the name of this issue itself points to an "interrupted conversion." If there is only a cleanup record for normal returns, the easiest state to miss is precisely the short interval after the interruption occurs. An outer fallback can still serve as a safeguard, but it should not be the only ownership record.

Successful and failed calls must leave different visible results. A successful call focuses on whether the image is returned as expected; a failed call focuses on whether there is still reviewable evidence of cleanup after the exceptional exit. "No further error was reported" cannot be treated as proof that the resources were released, and the fact that the final object can still be read cannot establish that the intermediate view had no lifecycle problem. The existing material does not provide a complete set of outputs, so these two statements define the review criteria, not the review results.

This also explains why the structure definitions are still worth retaining. `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, and `XImage` are entry points when returning to the X11 context, helping readers confirm that they are examining image conversion and event data rather than mistaking Region's geometric objects for the same layer. They do not prove the cleanup order; the cleanup order still has to be checked along the actual calls and exception paths.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> X11StructureReview
    X11StructureReview --> XShmInterruptedCleanup
    X11StructureReview --> RegionConstructionBoundary
    XShmInterruptedCleanup --> CAP211Review
    RegionConstructionBoundary --> CAP228Review
    CAP211Review --> [*]
    CAP228Review --> [*]
```

The branch in the diagram only represents the verification relationships retained by this history. It does not expand the structure declarations of `src/mss/linux.py` into a complete call chain, nor does it merge the two review entry points into one experiment.

## The Region Boundary Was Not Merged Along with It

The Region constructor normalization boundary has its own issue in this history: observation must begin with the pre-call state, confirming what visible changes remain after construction completes. "Normalization" here cannot be generalized into geometric rules for the entire capture flow; the record discusses only the boundary before and after the construction entry point and does not add a set of coordinate rules for other modules.

One option considered was to organize the input in the caller. This would keep the constructor simple and allow different callers to choose their own representations, but every entry point would have to repeat the same check, making it historically harder to tell which call had already been normalized. The other direction was to handle it uniformly at the constructor, with callers passing it the raw input; this is closer to the meaning of "boundary," but it requires confirming that existing callers do not depend on the old unnormalized state.

The current history records the approach of "confirm at the construction boundary, then decide whether to unify." This does not say that all inputs have already been converted in the constructor; it rejects declaring the migration complete without a before-and-after comparison. The pre-call state, the visible state after construction, and whether any additional side effects were produced should be recorded separately. If only the final Region is retained, it is impossible to determine whether the change came from the construction itself or from an earlier caller.

This decision also retains one compatibility cost: having callers organize the input distributes the old behavior across multiple entry points, while having the constructor organize it uniformly may change callers that depend on the old state. Neither cost can be estimated from the structure declarations. The current material supports only separating the entry points from the objects being observed first; it does not yet support declaring that either approach covers all callers.

## Later Review Entry Points

A subsequent addendum formally separated the two threads. The local records CAP-211 point to the reproduction scenario for interrupted XShm and require the visible results of one successful call and one failed call to be recorded separately; it entered an in-progress state in later actions, but that does not mean this page has obtained complete experimental results. It is cited here to show that the XShm review moved from a conceptual issue to a concrete entry point.

CAP-228 are responsible for the Region constructor normalization boundary. Their entry point begins with the pre-call state and observes whether any additional visible change remains after completion. This issue shares the compatibility-train background with XShm, but it does not share the same acceptance sample; putting the results from CAP-228 into the XShm cleanup section would again confuse the two boundaries. The two cards retain their own observation objects separately.

The adjacent material from the interface review is DOC-21. It discusses deterministic temporary XShm view release and is adjacent to this page's interrupted-cleanup direction, but this page does not copy the interface review's conclusions as implementation conclusions. When the release timing needs to be checked, follow through from there; when the state before and after Region construction needs to be confirmed, return to the entry points CAP-228.

## Old Wording That Was Retained

The old records contain three statements that are easy to keep repeating. The first is, "The issue points to `src/mss/linux.py`, so the modification must be here"; it was retained as navigational wording and is no longer treated as an ownership determination. The second is, "As long as conversion failure throws an exception, it is considered closed"; this is incompatible with the need to observe the resource state after an interruption, so it is marked obsolete. The third is, "Region normalization and XShm cleanup can be verified at once"; it does not distinguish image resources from construction inputs and is now retained in the history, but not as part of the current plan.

These old statements were not deleted because they explain why the later reviews must be performed twice. After deletion, readers would see only two tasks that had already been separated and would not see why they were initially placed together. They also should not be polished into current operating steps: the value of this material lies in preserving how the judgment at the time was narrowed down, not in providing a complete tutorial for a new implementation.

## Decisions Retained Currently

Within the confirmable scope, there are three decisions. First, interrupted XShm conversion cleanup centers on the resource state after the exceptional exit, with successful return serving only as a comparison. Second, the Region constructor normalization boundary confirms the changes before and after the call separately, without combining acceptance because the issues share a Linux file or the same compatibility train. Third, `src/mss/linux.py` continues to serve as the entry point for X11 structures and historical lookup, but a complete call chain cannot be derived from these declarations alone.

These three points are the local decisions this history can support. They do not replace the specific reviews, nor do they add the failure outputs that have not yet been obtained to the main text. If new results become available later, they should be placed back in the corresponding XShm or Region record, preserving which old judgment they change; do not recombine the two issues under a single "compatibility cleanup" title.

The remaining lookup order is short: first review the X11 structure declarations in `src/mss/linux.py`, then use CAP-211 to distinguish the successful and interrupted scenarios; when the state before and after construction is involved, go to CAP-228; when the temporary XShm view-release interface is involved, check DOC-21. This order describes the relationship among the historical materials; it is not a commitment about implementation ownership.

# XShm Temporary View Release Proposal

The Linux capture path in Aperture 11 needs a defined release point for temporary XShm image views. The concern is not normal screenshot completion, but conversion being interrupted after the view has been created: the slot is still there, and the next capture sees state left over from the previous one.

Compare two approaches first: have the conversion caller release the view at the end, or attach a release action to the temporary view when it is created. The former requires fewer changes, but every early return needs to include the release; the latter puts responsibility at the object boundary, making it easier to keep exception paths consistent with the normal path.

This draft favors the latter. We need to confirm whether there is an observable gap between view creation and shared-memory slot acquisition, and whether shutdown order affects subsequent captures.

# XShm Temporary View Release Plan

This change addresses a narrow boundary in Linux capture: a temporary XShm image view has already been handed to the conversion process, but the conversion does not reach its usual completion point. An early draft framed the issue as "add one release at the end"; that wording is no longer used after review. The end is only one path, not the boundary of resource ownership. As long as release depends on the caller reaching some tail point, a conversion exception, an early return, or an interruption after the data view is created can each leave a different result.

The entry point is still traced back from `src/mss/linux.py`. The declarations for `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, and `XImage` show that this file also owns the ctypes boundaries for the display connection, error structures, cursor image, and image view; do not spread responsibility for the temporary view across these adjacent structures. `XRRCrtcInfo`, `XRRModeInfo`, and `XRRScreenResources` are display-resource neighbors in the same file and do not share a close timing with this release plan.

The behavior recorded by CAP-212 is to reproduce the abnormal post-temporary-processing state from the pre-call state, then check after completion whether any additional visible changes remain. This description is not enough to assert which low-level step failed, but it is enough to rule out an acceptance criterion of "no leak as long as the screenshot succeeds": normal completion and incomplete conversion within the same capture must converge to the same slot state.

## Proposed boundary

Treat the shared-memory slot as a resource acquired by a capture, and the temporary image view as a short-lived borrow of that resource. Establish the release association immediately after the view is created, rather than relying on the conversion code to reach its last line. This does not let the view decide how the connection is closed; the connection, shared-memory slot, and conversion view remain three separate layers, each responsible only for the object it acquired.

The implementation should retain an explicit `_release_shm_slot` path where normal completion, conversion failure, and the close flow converge. The name itself is not a new public interface; it simply lets code review locate the action that "an acquired slot must be returned." When the view has been created but the conversion has not yet obtained a pixel result, the release association should be established before any subsequent processing that could be interrupted. If the data-view local is named `img_mv`, it must not be the sole criterion for whether the slot is released: the local's existence does not mean the conversion completed, and its absence does not mean the slot was not acquired.

An alternative is to use `try/finally` only in the conversion caller. Its advantage is that the flow is obvious; its drawback is that every call site receiving a temporary view must duplicate the same responsibility, and newly added early-exit points can easily bypass preparation steps outside `finally`. After review, using a caller-side convention as the primary approach is not recommended; callers may still clean up local objects within their own scope, but they do not own final responsibility for returning the shared-memory slot.

Another alternative is to wait until the outer facade finishes and clean everything up there. This approach was rejected. The outer layer can see only that one capture has ended; it cannot reliably distinguish whether this conversion has already established a temporary view. Deferring cleanup to the facade would also carry the impact of an interruption forward until before the next capture, which is inconsistent with the "no additional changes after completion" observation in CAP-212.

## Counterexamples to review

- The image request has completed, then an exception occurs before conversion. The slot must still be released; do not wait for the pixel object to be constructed.
- The conversion is interrupted after the temporary view is created. The release action must be executable once; re-entering the close path must not return the same slot twice.
- After normal conversion completes, the release association has already run. Subsequent close handling should process only resources still held by the connection layer and must not process the returned slot again.
- When MIT-SHM itself can no longer be used, failure recording and cleanup must not overwrite each other. The existing name `_shm_report_issue` is suitable to retain as the reporting entry point, but this plan does not treat reporting as a substitute for resource release.

Here, "certainty" means that the same type of temporary view has the same return result along the paths above; it does not require assigning all X11 errors to one cause. `XErrorEvent` can help locate the structural form of a server-side error, but it cannot establish that the shared-memory slot has been safely released.

## Change scope and rollback

The first round of changes should touch only the adjacent code in `src/mss/linux.py` between acquiring the shared-memory slot, establishing the temporary image view, and ending the conversion. Display-resource queries, the cursor image, and the XRandR structure are out of scope. If tracing shows that the temporary view does not hold a independently releasable slot, or that associating release before the low-level request completes breaks normal reads, roll back the "bind release when the view is created" point, retain the explicit slot ledger, and determine the association point again.

Before submission, cover normal conversion, conversion failure, interruption after view creation, and repeated capture separately from the same pre-call state. The focus is the slot state at the end of each path, not just a comparison of pixel content. DOC-22 concerns primary display selection and fallback; it should not be responsible for judging shared-memory lifetime.

# Primary Monitor Selection Troubleshooting Tree

## Start by separating the symptoms
This page covers the stage after the monitor list has entered the capture flow, when the primary monitor selection result needs to be checked. Do not categorize every case of "the image is wrong" here. First divide what you observed this time into three categories:

- The list contains monitors, but the expected primary entry was not selected;
- The list has no directly usable primary entry, and the flow enters fallback;
- The monitor list itself is incomplete, empty, or contains unexplained duplicates for the same batch of inputs.

For each review, retain at least the original list, each entry's name, the primary monitor flags, the object ultimately selected, and the runtime environment. Simply writing "the wrong one was selected" is not enough, because selection errors and list retrieval errors can look very similar to the caller.

## Follow this tree when on call

```text
Start
 │
 ├─ Can the monitors list be retrieved?
 │    ├─ No → Stop at list retrieval, retain the failure symptoms, and do not proceed to fallback evaluation
 │    └─ Yes
 │
 ├─ Does the list contain any entries flagged as the primary monitor?
 │    ├─ One entry → Compare it with the final selection; if they match, continue checking the region; if not, retain both objects
 │    ├─ Multiple entries → Do not pick one yourself; record all flags and the selection result
 │    └─ None → Record the actual fallback object; do not mark this as passing just because "there is an image"
 │
 └─ Can the result be reproduced with the same input?
      ├─ Yes → Hand the input, selection result, and environment to the current assignee
      └─ No → Stop expanding the scope of changes and add a raw record
```

Here, "list retrieval" means the boundary where the backend exposes the monitor list to the facade; do not confuse it with screenshot region calculation. First confirm what `monitors` returned, then examine how the selector uses those objects. Names are only for identification and comparison; do not use a human-readable name in place of the object itself as the sole basis for judgment.

## When there is a primary entry
If the list contains only one clearly identified primary monitor, record that entry's `name` and primary monitor flag, then compare it with the object ultimately returned. If the returned result differs, retain the list and selection result first; do not immediately change fallback. The question to answer here is "was the flagged entry given priority in selection," not "did pixels appear on the screen."

If the flagged entry matches the final object, continue checking whether the subsequent region still uses this object. If the region is wrong, keep the issue on the region calculation side; do not rewrite primary monitor selection just to place the image at the target position. The current records do not provide a consistent conclusion about coordinate origins across environments, so coordinates looking correct once cannot replace checking the selection result.

When multiple primary monitor flags appear, stop automatic correction. Save the list order, every flag, and the final object together. A change in list order without a change in the input objects is behavior that needs separate confirmation; do not document "the first entry" as the primary monitor rule unless there is clear evidence from this review to support it.

## When there is no primary entry
Having no entries flagged as the primary monitor does not mean fallback is correct. First record the object actually returned; if no object was returned, explicitly record the empty result as well. Then distinguish between two cases: the list exists but lacks flags, and the list was not successfully retrieved. In the former case, you can continue investigating the selection branch; in the latter, return to the retrieval point for `monitors`.

Older records place the entry point at `src/tests/test_implementation.py`. This can help locate nearby tests or examples, but the file location does not establish where fallback is implemented. In practice, if further searching from this path only reveals test-level details, stop broadening the search along that path and instead retain this input and result. Repeatedly swapping in the same input will not improve your ability to judge the issue.

If fallback returns an object, recording why it was selected is still required at this point. If there is no reason, no stable input, or no way to reproduce the result, do not document this result as the default behavior. You can initially describe the issue as "a certain object is returned when there is no primary flag," but do not add unconfirmed ordering, platform differences, or priorities.

## Three failures that are easy to conflate

### The list is empty
When the list is empty, first confirm whether an empty list was actually returned or whether the list was not retrieved at an earlier step. If the logs or tests only record "no primary monitor," that is not enough to conclude that fallback was entered. Stop the investigation at the list retrieval result; do not interpret subsequent selection results yet.

### The list has content, but the selection does not match
In this case, retain each entry's object and flag, and write the "expected entry" and "actual entry" side by side. Do not capture only the names. Identical names, duplicate list entries, or insufficient object fields can all make name comparisons misleading. There is currently no material supporting a more specific duplicate resolution rule, so leave this as an unresolved item if it occurs.

### The selection looks correct, but the caller still behaves abnormally
First review the selection result and the subsequent capture region separately. Primary monitor selection only answers "which one was selected"; by itself, it cannot establish whether the region offset, dimensions, or image returned by the backend are correct. If the list, flags, and final object all match, the next step is to preserve the state for handling on the region side, rather than adding new fallback rules to this page.

## Environment records
Review records must include the runtime environment; do not just write "works locally." At a minimum, distinguish the runtime platform, the backend used, the monitor list contents, and whether fallback was used. There is no requirement here to combine different environments into a single conclusion: if only one environment has records, document only the symptoms in that environment. If there are no results from a second environment, leave that unknown rather than summarizing it as "consistent across platforms."

When repeating the same input, retain the first list and selection result whenever possible. If the second result differs, record whether the difference is in the list, the primary flags, or the final object; do not combine the two results into an averaged description. If you cannot determine whether the difference comes from the environment or a change in input, stop expanding the scope of the review.

## Paths already tried that should not be pursued further
Earlier troubleshooting used the issue name and call name to point to `src/tests/test_implementation.py`. This path can still serve as a test entry point, but it cannot replace the records from this occurrence. Looking for the "correct fallback object" only by following file locations can easily lead to mistaking proximity to tests for the location of the implementation; if this happens, return to the last confirmed node in this page's tree.

Also, do not first adjust the caller's region parameters to hide selection differences. Even if this temporarily places the image at the expected position, it leaves you unable to determine whether the primary monitor was selected correctly. Restore the original input, save the list, flags, and final object again, and only then proceed.

## Handoff notation
CAP-213 is used to track additions to the missing runtime records for primary monitor. After the risk review, this issue still requires the actual test or example path to be written back to the card. The card was later transferred first to a teammate because the original owner was on leave; the handoff passes along records from the occurrence and unconfirmed items, not an unreviewed fallback conclusion.

When handing this to the next assignee, the body only needs to include four sets of values: whether the list was retrieved, the primary monitor flags, the object ultimately selected, and the runtime environment. If any item is missing, mark that item as "not recorded"; do not fill it in with speculation. If the result can be reproduced, also add the actual test or example path; if it cannot be reproduced, retain the state from the first occurrence and do not overwrite the failure record with a single successful run.

## Materials still needed
- A raw record from an occurrence with an empty list, including whether it actually entered fallback.
- A selection result from an occurrence where the list has content but no primary monitor flags.
- The handling result for an input with multiple primary flags.
- At least one review record that links the test entry point to the actual selection logic.

Until these materials are complete, this page can guide branching during an investigation, but it does not establish specific fallback ordering or cross-environment differences as fixed rules.

# Decision on Single-Strategy Facade Delegation

When the Aperture 11 compatibility train was first documented, the division of responsibilities between the facade and concrete strategies was reflected only in calling conventions, not in a recorded decision we could refer back to. There are two approaches available: have the facade choose separate handling paths for `monitors`, `cursor`, `region`, and screenshot data; or select one strategy at the start and delegate subsequent requests to that object.

The provisional decision is to use single-strategy facade delegation. The facade retains only strategy selection; the selected object handles monitor queries, the cursor, regions, and returned data within the same request. When tracing calls, we can then start with the selection result rather than guess from action names whether the implementation has switched again.

`src/mss/linux.py` is an existing reference point for a limited look at the Linux side. The file starts with ctypes structures such as `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, and `XImage`. These declarations show that the Linux side has its own type definitions, but they should not be taken to mean that each structure is an independent facade entry point.

Still to document: where `exit` and `close` sit after the strategy enters `context`; cleanup once screenshot data has been handed to the caller; and whether a missing action loops back to the facade for another selection.

# Facade Single-Strategy Delegation Decision

The initial version left a very narrow judgment: the Aperture 11 compatibility train should not split strategy selection into each capture action. At the time, it did not distinguish "strategy" from the structure declarations in the Linux file, nor explain why this choice was worth documenting separately. Looking back later, the issue was not any one X11 type, but when the facade makes its choice and whether it can switch to another object again because of the request name.

The earliest investigation started from `src/mss/linux.py`. What can be seen directly here are several ctypes structures: `Display` on line 51, `XErrorEvent` on line 58, `XFixesCursorImage` on line 74, and `XImage` on line 94; there are also `XRRCrtcInfo`, `XRRModeInfo`, and `XRRScreenResources` later. The file header contains `from __future__ import annotations`, `import os`, and `from contextlib import suppress`, and imports type definitions from `ctypes`.

This material is suitable for consulting local types and adjacent call material from the Linux side. It does not encode the facade's responsibilities in the structure names. During the initial reading, it was easy to infer an entire capture path upward from `Display` or `XImage`; this decision retains that entry point but no longer uses that reading as the basis for responsibility boundaries.

> Working statement from the draft: First find the Linux object, then look separately at the monitors, cursor, and screenshot paths; if every path works, the facade's selection point can be filled in later.

This sentence records the reading order at the time and also exposes the problem. Confirming local paths separately by action cannot answer whether the same facade request continues using the same strategy. It was later replaced by the decision below, but was not deleted because someone starting again from the Linux file later could still fall back into the same misreading.

## The two organizational approaches on the table at the time

The first approach was to have the facade dispatch each public action separately. When requesting `monitors`, it would select one handling point; when requesting `cursor`, it would follow another branch of logic; `region` and screenshot data would also be handled separately. This appeared close to the call names, and local changes could easily be placed near the corresponding methods.

The cost was that selection would no longer be a one-time operation. A caller would see the same capture facade, while internally the handler could be chosen again depending on the action. Which object supplied the monitor list, who interpreted the region, and whether the cursor and screenshot data still belonged to the same context would all have to be maintained through additional conventions. When compatibility changes landed in multiple places, investigation would first become a question of "who was actually selected this time?"

The second approach was to determine the strategy at the beginning of the facade and treat subsequent actions as a sequence of requests to that object. `monitors`, `cursor`, `region`, and screenshot data would not be selected again based on different names. The strategy could still use its own platform types, system resources, and local calls internally; the facade would not need to expand those differences into a second dispatch scheme.

This approach did not require all backends to share an implementation. The Linux strategy could be organized around the types in X11, while other platforms could use different resources and call forms. The decision constrains the facade's delegation relationship, rather than turning the underlying code into a shared cross-platform path.

## Decision

Adopt **single-strategy facade delegation**: a facade request first selects one strategy; within the scope of that request, monitor queries, cursor requests, region handling, and screenshot data are all handled by that selected object. The facade's job is to select and forward, not to select a strategy again for subsequent actions.

"Single-strategy" does not describe the number of objects, nor does it require the strategy to contain only one function. It only limits the number of selections made when a public request passes through the facade. A strategy may delegate its work to local helper objects, or enter different internal calls based on platform capabilities; those branches do not constitute another selection by the facade.

The state diagram below records the delegation outline that this decision intends to preserve. It is not a function call graph for the Linux backend, and it does not list the fields of every structure in `src/mss/linux.py`.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Select strategy
    Select strategy --> Selected strategy
    Selected strategy --> Monitor request : monitors
    Selected strategy --> Cursor request : cursor
    Selected strategy --> Region request : region
    Selected strategy --> Screenshot request
    Monitor request --> Selected strategy
    Cursor request --> Selected strategy
    Region request --> Selected strategy
    Screenshot request --> Return data
    Return data --> Exit context : context
    Exit context --> [*]
```

The return to "Selected strategy" in the diagram means that the request is still handled by the same object; it does not mean these actions must occur in the order shown in the diagram. A call to Fang Ke may only retrieve the monitor list, or may request a region screenshot; what matters for this decision is that an already-started request does not switch from the facade to another strategy merely because the entry-point name is different.

## Responsibility boundaries

| Location | Responsibility retained by this decision |
| --- | --- |
| capture facade | Select a strategy at the start of the request and forward subsequent actions to the selection result |
| Selected strategy | Handle requests related to `monitors`, `cursor`, `region`, and screenshot data, while maintaining the local execution relationship |
| `src/mss/linux.py` | Provide Linux-side type declarations and their local adjacent material, including `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, and `XImage` |
| Caller | Initiate requests and consume returned data, without assembling strategy selection independently based on platform details |

This responsibility table intentionally does not attach facade semantics to the Linux structures. Names such as `XRRScreenResources` can be used to return to the file and continue reading, but do not automatically indicate that it is the public boundary for monitor queries; likewise, the appearance of `XFixesCursorImage` in the file does not mean that the facade should maintain a separate platform route for cursor.

## Why not dispatch by action

The appeal of dispatching by action is that each entry point looks like an independent small change. For `monitors`, one can focus only on the list; for `cursor`, only on the cursor; for `region`, only on coordinates; and screenshot data can be handled separately. This decomposition is useful when reading a particular piece of local code, but it turns the same request at the facade layer into several opportunities for reselection.

During compatibility consolidation, those opportunities increase the cost of explanation. If monitor queries and screenshot actions each select their own strategy, the relationship between the list received by the caller and the object actually captured must be explained separately. If the cursor is placed on another facade branch, the cursor request leaves the context of the selected strategy. If region handling is rerouted by the facade, selection is no longer a one-time decision made at the start of the request.

These are not attributions of any existing error, but structures to avoid when comparing the options. We did not write into the decision that "every action must have the same implementation steps"; we only avoid having the facade make another strategy judgment on the grounds of the action name.

Conversely, the strategy does not need to eliminate platform branches to satisfy this decision. The Linux-side types related to `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XImage`, or XRandR remain in the local Linux context. Single-strategy delegation does not elevate them into general-purpose facade objects, nor does it require other strategies to copy these declarations.

## Relationship to context

The draft mentioned `context`, `exit`, and `close`, but there was not enough material at the time to write the closing order as an interface commitment. This version still does not invent a specific order. The decision retains only one checkable boundary: after a strategy is selected, its entry, processing, and exit should not be split into unrelated object relationships because the facade reroutes a particular action.

Therefore, when examining a request, first record the object selected by the facade, then inspect which local steps the request passes through within that object. To continue examining Linux resource details, start with the structure declarations and file-header imports in `src/mss/linux.py`. The appearance of `suppress` indicates that the file has local context utilities, but that import alone cannot replace judgment about the closing path.

Returned data belongs to the same boundary. The work item CAP-216 brings this judgment back into an actual call inspection. Its goal is to find the most recent call reported as single-strategy facade delegation and fill in the call method and the result seen by the user. What it is suited to verify is whether the selected object continuously handles the request, not to register every X11 name in the Linux file one by one.

Do not write an as-yet-unseen call result as a conclusion in advance.

`src/mss/linux.py` remains a Linux-side reference point, not the only entry point. The actual verification can begin with the declarations of `Display`, `XErrorEvent`, `XFixesCursorImage`, and `XImage`, then return to the facade's selection result. This preserves the local type context in the file while avoiding inferring cross-layer responsibilities from type names.

- The layer at which a public request should produce a result when the strategy lacks a capability has not been expanded in this decision.
- The exit path for `context` and its specific pairing with `exit` and `close` still needs to be examined together with the selected strategy's implementation.
- The way exceptions are surfaced during local resource cleanup after a request returns screenshot data is not decided here.

These open items do not change the delegation decision already made. If they later turn out to require the facade to select a strategy again, they should be handled as a revision of this decision; if they are merely resource handling within a strategy, they should remain in the corresponding implementation record.

# Proposal for Rejecting Unknown Windows Strategies

Aperture 11 compatibility train first ran into an entry-point choice: when Windows strategy is passed a name with no corresponding implementation, should it stop at strategy selection, or continue passing it to `src/mss/windows.py`, and wait for a later Windows operation to fail.

At the time, the latter was preferred. The reason was simple: avoid adding a check at the entry point. Existing callers might contain names that had not yet been cleaned up, and delaying failure might not change the behavior of the selection layer. But this was only a working assumption; we had not yet verified which layer's error would allow the caller to distinguish a name problem.

This round compares two paths:

- Identify unknown names at Windows strategy selection and reject them before entering the specific implementation.
- Keep the existing selection path, pass the name to `src/mss/windows.py`, and let a subsequent initialization or system call expose the failure.

The experiment is limited to unknown Windows strategies. Known strategies, aliases, default selection, and underlying GDI errors remain unchanged. We need to confirm that rejection preserves the requested name, and that an actual Windows API failure is not misclassified as a strategy selection failure.

If the upfront check incorrectly affects existing names, withdraw the added check and keep the delayed-failure path. Whether aliases should be registered as official strategies will be decided after call samples are available.

# Proposal for Rejecting Unknown Windows Strategies

This review record does not start with Windows API itself, but with whether a name should be blocked before it enters the Windows implementation. The early draft treated an unknown strategy as an internal backend issue: the entry point would do one fewer check, pass the name down, and let initialization or a system call fail eventually. There was no caller evidence supporting this assumption, but it explains why "delayed failure" was considered the smaller-change option at the time.

The local material found is `src/mss/windows.py`. The file header directly contains `ctypes`, `sys`, and imports including `POINTER`, `WINFUNCTYPE`, `Structure`, `c_int`, and `c_void_p`. This shows that the code sits next to Windows interop code, but the file location alone cannot prove that strategy names should be interpreted through the GDI path. Putting "no such strategy" and "Windows call failed" in the same error chain is still the key distinction this review needs to make.

## Candidate Boundaries

Candidate A: validate the Windows strategy at strategy selection. If the name is unrecognized, stop before entering the concrete backend operation; known names continue along the original delegation path. The benefit is that the error stays close to the request, so the caller does not have to pass through Windows initialization to learn that the name is unsupported. The cost is that the selection point must know which names are supported, and this check must also be updated when aliases are added later.

Candidate B: continue passing the name to `src/mss/windows.py`. The change stays near the backend, and the selection point does not need to know more names; the cost is that an unknown name may appear as an initialization failure or a low-level call failure, so the symptom seen by the caller depends on the branch actually taken. Candidate B can remain a compatibility fallback, but the backend's ability to throw an error does not mean strategy validation has been completed.

Mapping an unknown name to a default strategy was also discussed. That direction was not tested: it would turn a spelling error into an apparently successful capture and would not show whether the object requested by the caller actually exists. This review is not aimed at capturing something on screen wherever possible, so default mapping is not counted as a compatibility option.

## Planned Verification

First prepare a Windows strategy with no corresponding implementation, and record whether it stops before delegation and whether the error text still includes the requested name. Then use a known name as a control to confirm that the new check does not interrupt normal selection; after that, observe a real Windows call-failure path to confirm that the backend's existing error handling is not swallowed by the entry-point branch. The comparison is about error layers, not image content.

The most practical disagreement in the review is the scope of the change. Early rejection makes it easier to say that "the name is not recognized," but it exposes the risk that historical aliases have not yet been cataloged; delayed failure is more conservative at the entry point, but mixes up request errors with environment or API errors. The current material has no alias list and no caller sample showing that an unregistered name is in use, so the supported-name set cannot be hard-coded as a complete table.

If this round adopts Candidate A, it will add only a rejection branch for an unknown Windows strategy; it will not reorder known strategies, change the default selection, or rewrite handling of Windows API failures. If the comparison review finds that an existing name is rejected incorrectly, the rollback condition is to remove the corresponding pre-check and temporarily return to Candidate B's delayed-failure behavior; it must not be silently changed to the default strategy. If known names delegate as usual, unknown names stop before the concrete implementation, and lower-level failures still occur along the original path, the experiment is complete.

This page still retains the early judgment that "the backend failing eventually is sufficient," because it is part of the proposal's history and should not be read as the current Windows strategy list. Continue the investigation from the entry point of `src/mss/windows.py` and the direct interop code; the available material is insufficient to add specific names, aliases, or caller dependencies yet.

# mss Caller Alternative Route Proposal

This proposal preserves an approach that was not adopted at the time. It was originally placed beside the integration discussion in mss-client-integration, but people continued to reach it through old links, so the original uncertainty, objections, and unfilled trial window were left in place. It is not the current integration guide; in particular, the leaning below toward `CoreGraphics handle` must not be read as a route that has been implemented.

## The Platform Name Wasn't What Blocked It

The initial comparison was narrow: continue handling caller integration testing through `X11 capability`, or split `CoreGraphics handle` into a separate section. The former made it easier to look back through the old entry point; the latter aimed to keep the two failure paths from being mixed together in one place. The draft's "different exits" only meant that the failure paths recorded in the two pieces of material were different; it did not establish that they produced different results for all caller samples.

At the time, the preference for splitting was not because a better unified interface had already been found. The only thing that could be confirmed then was that callers would bring integration feedback back to the same place, while the observed failures might not come from the same entry point. If both sides were still handled under one generic capability name, the feedback would be written up as the same kind of problem, and adding the original inputs later would be difficult. This was the proposal's starting point, not a conclusion drawn after a completed run.

The candidate `capture facade` was therefore only a proposed isolation layer. It should put the old route and the candidate route side by side, so caller samples could still be traced back to their respective entry points. The draft did not commit to moving all callers over, nor did it say that this layer could replace the existing adapter boundary. If those statements were made too categorically, a rollback would make it harder to tell which part came from the trial and which had already been in the old entry point.

## The Originally Proposed Short Trial

A two-week window was proposed: one group would remain on the old, unadopted route, and the other would use candidate `capture facade`. Both sides should retain the same caller samples, inputs, and observation window, and record the original inputs, the version used, and the first result observed. The purpose of this arrangement was only to compare whether splitting the entry points reduced confusion, not to predetermine a winner for either side.

The draft specifically required changing only one condition in the comparison. If one side changed its entry point while the other also changed its input or caller, any differences seen later could not be attributed to the split itself. During review, someone asked to add an opposing input to confirm that the conclusion would not hold only for one-sided samples; that validation window was never completed and should remain blank.

There was also no start date or stable handoff owner at the time. Therefore, "two weeks" was only the intended observation length and should not be interpreted as two weeks of caller integration testing having taken place. Without feedback from real callers, the proposer could only organize the recording format; they could not use that to declare the candidate entry point adopted.

## Objections Listed at the Time

The objections first centered on the success criteria. A single pass, changing only the display label, or a green result with no real caller sample would all be insufficient grounds for changing the entry point. If pinpointing the caller did not get faster or misclassification did not decrease, keeping two entry points would only make integrators guess one more time.

Another issue was the rollback path. The original draft said: once the candidate route caused feedback that could not be explained, end the trial and restore the original entry point. But "restore the original entry point" did not say whether to roll back only `capture facade`, or also roll back `CoreGraphics handle`, which had already been split out. This is not something copyediting can fill in; the two scopes would affect which section callers return to and whether the old material could still be reviewed as-is.

Therefore, the candidate route should not extend beyond the existing interface to add a larger unified solution. What the integration side actually needs is to keep feedback next to an identifiable entry point, not create another set of names that would require long-term maintenance for a single trial. This constraint also explains why the old draft did not provide a comprehensive migration table: even the rollback scope had not been decided at the time.

## Later Addendum

The adjacent CAPA-003 once had an incorrect association: the expiration action was placed on this card, then it was confirmed not to belong to the "handoff record following the triggering of mss · Client Integration" and was moved back to the original thread. The card had reproduction steps left on it, but this only corrected the ownership of the handoff record; it cannot be used to prove the effect of the candidate route or to stand in for the missing trial window.

This addendum, in turn, illustrates one concern in the old proposal: integration records with similar names are easily merged into the same place, while the underlying situation may not be the same. The CAPA-003 reference is retained here only to explain why that incorrect association was not carried forward; it is not acceptance evidence for this alternative route.

## Still Unresolved

The original draft did not provide a list of "callers currently in use," nor did it record who would confirm the rollback scope during rollback. Neither item can be filled in from later links. If this route is reconsidered, first confirm whether the old entry point is still the actual integration point, then decide the boundary of the candidate layer separately; the old proposal itself records only this sequence, not any results from work that was actually carried out.

The entry point for the related material is still `docs/adj-mss/proposals/unused-mss-client-integration-approach.md`. This page preserves the leaning toward splitting and the incomplete trial conditions for reviewing why the route was not written up as an established plan at the time.
