# Quality Signal Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

When the quality signal desk gets stuck, first treat it as an incident record whose boundaries have not yet been clarified, rather than a defect awaiting a conclusion. Start with the material from the first anomaly at the current entry point: what the input was, what version was in use at the time, and where the earliest failure or nonzero exit code appeared. None of these three can be inferred backward from a later successful run.

This page covers failure samples, regression stratification, and attribution of unstable signals around Monitor and capture-region models. It does not fix functionality for the current entry point, nor does it restore paths that have already been disabled for the caller. If new permissions, interface changes, or explanations of cross-project behavior are needed, retain the material already collected and hand the issue off.

## Choose one path first; do not guess in parallel

```text
Current entry point is stuck
│
├─ No initial raw record
│  └─ Collect the missing material; stop if no material is available
│
├─ Initial record exists, but no pre-failure state
│  └─ Work backward to recover the last verifiable state; do not attribute the cause yet
│
└─ Both are available
   │
   ├─ The first difference appears after changing only the adjacent models-quality-signal
   │  └─ The quality signal desk continues handling it
   │
   ├─ The current entry point, exit action, or original job changed first
   │  └─ Hand off to the entry point maintainers, with the original job and exit code attached
   │
   ├─ Monitor was at a different point in time, so the old conclusion cannot be matched
   │  └─ Retain the old conclusion, compare the two points in time, and do not overwrite the old record
   │
   ├─ Restricted details need to be opened or permissions changed
   │  └─ Hand off to the permission maintainers; do not guess the root cause from missing pages
   │
   └─ The first difference still cannot be found
      └─ Stop at the raw record; do not close the issue based on a green rerun
```

Each level of the tree answers only one question. Without a raw record, there is no way to know whether "stuck" means the input did not arrive, the test did not start, or the result was not written back; without the last verifiable state before the failure, there is also no way to determine whether the anomaly occurred before or after entering the quality signal desk. Do not collect both kinds of missing material at the same time and then mix them together as though they came from the same run.

### Raw record missing

When the current entry point reports only "stuck" without a raw record, first collect an incident package that can be matched to subsequent material. Clearly document in the package: the current entry point identifier, the original input, the version in use at the time, the first visible failure, whether there is an exit code, and whether this record came from the original job. If only a compiled summary is available, it may be attached, but it cannot replace the raw output.

Do not change the input while collecting the missing material. Replaying the adjacent models-quality-signal and replaying the original input are two different things: the former is used to find the input boundary, while the latter is used to confirm whether the same incident conditions still exist. Which one comes first depends on what material is missing, not on which one is easier to turn green.

If the incident conditions have already disappeared before the missing material is collected, the record should say "the initial failure sample was not retained". Do not rewrite the last passing run as evidence that the original incident has recovered, and do not describe a historical failure as a verified model issue. At this point, only the current entry point, the available version, and the missing items can be handed off.

If the pre-failure state is also missing, look back for the last state that can be confirmed. Here, "can be confirmed" means inputs, test logs, trace snippets, or diff snippets already present in the source material, not inferences filled in based on later results. Filling in one preceding state is enough; if there is no continuous material further back, leave the gap in the record.

CAPB-010 previously required filling in the state one step before the failure. This item was later canceled because the caller had stopped using that path and no further fix was scheduled. Canceling the fix does not mean the pre-failure state at the time can be deleted; the existing evidence can still serve to clarify the boundaries at handoff, but there is no longer a requirement to fix it into a usable path.

### Comparison after the first record is available

Once the first record and the pre-failure state are available, first find the "first point of difference." Use this fixed comparison order: whether the current entry point is the same, whether the input is the same, whether Monitor is at the same point in time, and only then the contents of models-quality-signal. Do not infer what happened in between from the final display, averages, or regression summaries.

Change only one condition in each round of comparison. The constraint in CAPB-016 is to swap only one adjacent models-quality-signal, leaving the remaining current entry point and entry point unchanged. Only differences obtained this way can be retained on the quality signal board: if the first change between the original input and the adjacent input occurs immediately after signal processing, record both inputs, their shared current entry point, and the first result for each, then continue investigating regression stratification or unstable-signal attribution.

If the input, version, and entry point were all changed during the comparison, the result can only show that the three differ in combination, not that any one of them is the cause. Do not delete these runs, but mark them as "not usable for localization"; return to a record with fewer retained conditions and start again. Do not collapse multiple changes into a single "environment difference" to save time.

Once a baseline has been recorded, its purpose is to provide a common reference for later samples, not to authorize all subsequent green results to overwrite the initial failure. CAPB-005 reminds us to first find the first recorded result from the current entry point after the change; a subsequent green result only shows that the later run passed and cannot rewrite the contents of the first record. Keeping both side by side is the only way to tell whether the issue was transient, input-related, or a break in the record chain itself.

If there are still differences even though the current entry point is the same and the adjacent input has not changed, do not immediately label the issue as instability. First check the version used and Monitor's point in time. CAPB-015 left a check item for differences in Monitor timing, so the old conclusion must remain in its original location: it can still describe the sample from that time, but cannot be applied directly to Monitor at another point in time.

### Different Monitor points in time

For field instances of Monitor observed at different points in time, the handoff materials should retain at least the temporal context of each side: which side is the failure sample, which side is the comparable sample, which version each sample corresponds to, and the object the old conclusion originally referred to. Do not backfill newer information into the earlier sample and make it appear to have been known at the time.

If the old conclusion conflicts with the current sample, first note "The old conclusion applies only to the original point in time" next to the current record, then continue the assessment. The conflict itself is neither a failure nor a regression already confirmed by the quality signal desk; it only indicates that the samples cannot be compared directly. Comparison can continue only if there is at least one continuous, verifiable link connecting the input, current entry point, and version relationship.

If Monitor's timing discrepancy happens at the same time as an input replacement, initially treat it as a mixed change. Do not route it to models-quality-signal, and do not immediately hand it elsewhere just because the name contains Monitor. When no sample isolating an individual change is available, stop at "comparison conditions need to be separated"; preserve the existing samples and do not require the person taking over to infer backward from aggregate results.

### `strategy selection` is a stop point

Old field notes once described `strategy selection` as a location for follow-up inspection. It remains only a stop point: if it does not appear in the existing records, its status cannot be inferred from other fields; even if it does appear, that only indicates that the materials reached this node, not that it is known what it changed.

When troubleshooting can proceed only by relying on `strategy selection`, but the corresponding input, logs, or trace snippet is not available, make the handoff clearly state the comparisons already completed, the missing materials, and the location of the original records. Do not create an apparently continuous story by rerunning. If a new action would change a user-visible interface or require a cross-project decision, the quality signal desk is responsible only for handing over the current situation; subsequent steps must go through the formal review process separately.

This is intended to prevent two common misjudgments: first, seeing one rerun succeed and attributing the earlier failure to a temporary fluctuation; second, treating a directory or aggregate name as the actual processing location. The former loses the initial failure, while the latter skips materials that must exist. Neither situation can serve as a handoff conclusion.

### Exit codes and the original job

A non-zero exit code must be considered together with the original job. If an exit code is recorded on its own, the person taking over cannot determine whether it was produced by the current entry point, by the exit action, or by another run. CAPB-010 both note that a non-author followed the original checklist to the exit entry, received a non-zero exit code, and linked the exit entry and that exit code back to the original job. This is a reusable recording method.

When recording an exit code, attaching these three items is sufficient: the location of the original job, the last confirmed step before reaching the exit entry, and the location where the exit code first appeared. If the exit code disappears after a rerun, retain its first location and note that the later run was different. Do not leave only "recovered"; that states neither the original job nor whether the input or entry point was changed.

The exit action has already started, but when the Quality Signal Desk sees no input difference, hand it to the current entry point maintainer. Do not add speculation such as "the model may have a problem" when handing it over; that would insert an attribution that has not yet occurred into the handoff recipient's starting point. Conversely, if the exit action has not changed and the difference can be reproduced reliably by replacing only the adjacent models-quality-signal, keep it with the Quality Signal Desk for continued input comparison.

When the exit entry itself requires permission to view, do not record "cannot see it" as a failure. State that the restricted details have not yet been obtained, how far the original job is known to have progressed, and whether a nonzero exit code already exists, then hand it to the permissions maintainer. A party without permission should not interpret the exit action on behalf of the permissions maintainer.

### Paths Disabled by the Caller

Some old incidents will not enter the remediation queue. The reason CAPB-010 was canceled is that the caller had already disabled that path; in this case, the task is not to make the old path pass again, but to confirm whether an active current entry point still follows the same path.

If there is no active entry point, save the original sample, the state immediately before the failure, and the cancellation reason, then stop. Do not create new replay conditions just to prove that the old path "should continue working." If another active entry point still shows the same first failure, it is a new incident and a record should be created from the new entry point; the old card is for historical navigation only, and the two entry points must not be combined into a single conclusion.

A caller disabling a path does not mean that the Quality Signal Desk never received the issue. It only changes the remediation priority and handoff direction. The old sample can still help explain why the exit action at that time could not be treated as model attribution, but it cannot be used to claim that the current version still has the same impact.

### Who Gets It, and What to Hand Over

A handoff is not forwarding the entire troubleshooting text. The recipient needs the minimum material required to continue making a determination: the original failure sample, the last confirmed state before the failure, the only condition that changed in the comparison, and the stopping point. The handoff content differs by branch.

| Incident point | Recipient | Content to retain at handoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The first difference appears after changing only the adjacent models-quality-signal | Quality Signal Desk maintainer | The two inputs, the shared current entry point, the baseline, and the first difference |
| The current entry point changes first, or the exit code is attached to the original job | Current entry point maintainer | The original job, the state before the exit entry, and the first nonzero exit code |
| The Monitor points in time differ, so the old conclusion cannot be applied directly | Monitor-related maintainer | The two points in time, the corresponding versions, and the original context of the old conclusion |
| Restricted details or permission blocks further viewing | Permissions maintainer | Materials already obtained, missing details, and actions not taken |
| The caller has disabled the old path and there is no active entry point | Exit action | The original sample, the fact of deactivation, and the absence of a new remediation arrangement |

"Exit action" in the table means the condition for stopping further troubleshooting, not a person or a new issue. It applies when the caller has disabled the path, the first incident has already been lost, or new permission is required but has not yet been obtained. When stopping, the material location and the gaps must be left behind; the recipient is not required to continue following evidence that does not exist.

When handing off to the Quality Signal Desk, avoid writing "Please confirm whether this is unstable." State whether the comparison changed only one adjacent input, where the first difference occurred, and whether the baseline has been retained. When handing off to the maintainer of the current entry point, avoid attaching an overall assessment; the relationship between the original job and the exit code is more useful than a vague attribution.

CAPB-005, CAPB-015, and CAPB-016 can be used to review the initial result, the Monitor time point, and the adjacent-input replay, respectively; CAPB-010 retain the background on disabling the old path and recording exit codes. To fill in the timeline for an unresolved incident, see DOC-33, but do not copy that page's unconfirmed items into the handoff conclusions here.

### Actions during a shift that can easily compromise incident evidence

**Repeated reruns.** Rerunning immediately after the first failure often produces a different result. Copy the initial evidence before rerunning; after rerunning, label it as the second run, and do not replace the initial result with the second one. A green result is a new fact, not a revision of an old fact.

**Changing multiple conditions at once.** When the input, current entry point, and version all change together, the record is still valuable, but it only shows that a difference exists. Do not include such a record in a single-variable comparison for regression stratification, or use it to ask any one party to make a fix.

**Treating cancellation as recovery.** After the caller disables a path, cancellation of the related cards does not mean that the exit action has succeeded, nor does it mean that historical nonzero exit codes have disappeared. Cancellation only means that fixes for that path will no longer be scheduled; whether the active entry point is affected must be checked separately.

**Using missing permissions to fill in the story.** When restricted details have not been opened, the only thing that can be confirmed is "not yet obtained." Describing this as a permissions configuration error, an input that did not arrive, or a component failure goes beyond the available evidence. The most appropriate handoff at this point is to list the original job and raw records already obtained, along with the details that need to be viewed.

**Overwriting old conclusions.** When the Monitor time points differ, the old conclusion stays next to the old sample. A different assessment can be added for the current sample, but the old paragraph must not be rewritten as though it had always described the current version. This allows later comparisons to determine whether the difference comes from a change in the object or a change in the assessment.

### Additional notes on this round's evidence

In this round's records, the current result has been loaded, but the failure stopped after the person on duty. This statement can only describe the point the records had reached at the time; it cannot replace the initial failure sample. If the input, version, or exit code from before the person on duty was not retained, still treat this as "missing original records."

Results obtained after fixing the toolchain in place should also be retained alongside the initial failure. Fixing the toolchain in place is not a root-cause statement; it is only a condition added later. Adjacent-input replay began only after the baseline records were completed, so do not retroactively write replay observations into the earlier baseline description.

The work items started one after the other concern adjacent inputs and Monitor timing, respectively. Both being in progress does not mean they can be investigated together. The adjacent-input work still requires all other current entry points to remain unchanged; the Monitor timing work still requires the previous conclusions to be retained. Their relationship can only be described in a single record when the same batch of comparable material is available.

### Minimal format for a field report

Before each handoff, organize the information in the following order; there is no need to rewrite all historical material:

1. What is the current entry point, and where is the first failed sample.
2. What is the last confirmable state before the failure; if there is none, explicitly state that it is missing.
3. What was the only change in this comparison. If there was no single change, write "mixed changes".
4. Whether a correspondence has emerged between the original job, the exit entry point, and a nonzero exit code.
5. Whether Monitor is at the same point in time as in the previous conclusions.
6. Where work stopped: missing raw records, missing permissions, waiting for an input comparison, or the caller having disabled the path.

This field report does not need to speculate about the ultimate cause. Its purpose is to let the person taking over continue from the first gap, rather than guess all over again from the compiled conclusions.

- [ ] Follow the action routing in CAPD-009 to find a handoff owner; do not include retired groups in new entry points.

"Final output" here does not mean a success message in a log. Before closing the window, verify the actual artifact or status produced by `capture facade` and save it separately from the first visible result. If there are only logs and no artifact or status, the checklist item does not pass.

# wheel cut window discussion notes

The desktop team needs to choose a deliverable scope between retaining the current facade entry point and adjusting the window; the dispute is not about creating a separate entry point, but how far release approval should extend in this round.

# Wheel cut window decision record

This record is retained because "retain the current facade entry first" in the initial draft was later interpreted as a long-term architectural judgment. That was not what it meant. At the time, the wheel cut needed to determine which changes could enter during the release window and which changes could not be allowed through along with the window; whether the entry should be rearranged later was not decided at that meeting.

The initial draft was not deleted or altered. The contemporaneous judgment it recorded still applies: window adjustment and facade entry changes are two things that may be related, but cannot be jointly confirmed through the same sentence. Retaining the entry means not changing the handoff point first this round merely to expand the change surface; window adjustment only means that the local portions covered by existing material can proceed. When the two statements are put together, they are easily compressed into "the window will not change" or "the entry is already finalized." Both interpretations go further than the decision made at the time.

This addendum does not reclassify the window proposal or revise the old judgment into current operating instructions. What should be retained is the boundary set at the time, the approaches the review did not accept, and why those approaches did not become conditions for the wheel cut.

## The decision in the initial draft

There were only three parts to the decision at the time.

First, the current facade entry would continue to handle the portions that needed to be closed out this round. This choice avoided turning one release window into an entry migration at the same time; it did not declare the current entry to be the only entry, much less reject any possible window adjustment in the future.

Second, window-related changes would be handled according to the scope covered by the existing material. Local actions supported by the material could enter this round; portions not covered by the material would remain as open points. Here, "coverage" does not mean writing a conclusion with sufficient confidence. It means that a reader can return to the relevant call site and reassess whether the action actually belongs to this change.

Third, unconfirmed cross-platform relationships would not be inserted into the release conclusion. The question left at the end of the initial draft—whether the same call chain could be used for verification across different operating systems—was left precisely because locating something on the Windows side does not automatically show that other environments have the same relationship. The end of the cut will not make this question disappear on its own.

There was a gap in the initial draft's wording: it said "retain the entry," but did not repeatedly note that this was a narrowing action for this round. As a result, when it was cited later, some people carried away only the first half and misrepresented the temporary narrowing as design ownership. This update restores that context without revoking the original decision.

## The two paths compared at the review table

One path was to continue narrowing the scope through the current facade entry. Its advantage was not that it proved the entry was better, but that it limited the judgments this round had to take on to the scope that could already be inspected. The window issue did not need to be declared resolved because of this; relationships for which there was no material did not need to be disguised as a completed migration in the cut. The cost was equally clear: the open points would remain, and if the window were reopened for adjustment later, the work would still need to begin with the call relationships and maintenance ownership.

The other path was to adjust the window and handle the entry relationship along with it. Its appeal was that, on the surface, it could organize two concepts at once: the change to the window and the ownership of the entry might appear to become consistent in the same change. But once this path entered review, the discussion would no longer concern only a particular window object. It would also require an explanation of where the call starts, how platform branches are handled, and who would continue maintaining it after the change ended. Without this material, "adjust them together" would merely put several unconfirmed points into one larger action.

The second path was not rejected at the time. What was rejected was making it a prerequisite for this round's wheel cut. Direction and timing needed to be recorded separately: the review did not say that the entry could not be changed later, nor that window adjustment had no value; it only concluded that the existing material could not support approving both together within the release window.

Another proposal was to split the window adjustment into more small pieces and place each piece into the cut separately. This idea did not produce a new decision at the time. Splitting can reduce the surface area of an individual change, but it cannot supply the missing call chain or automatically fill in cross-platform verification and subsequent maintenance ownership. If every small piece still depends on the same unconfirmed relationship, splitting it more finely only makes the judgments appear more numerous; it does not actually make them more complete.

The opposing proposal was to delay the entire wheel cut and act only after all potentially relevant platforms could receive the same explanation. That did not become the result of this round either. The review adopted a narrower boundary: the scope supported by existing material could proceed, while the uncovered portions would remain undecided. This boundary did not require exhausting every platform at once, but it did require that local approval not be written as global confirmation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[wheel cut window] --> B{Existing verifiable material}
    B -->|yes| C[Retain current facade entry]
    C --> D[Approve only the scope covered by existing evidence]
    B -->|no| E[Defer window adjustment]
```

In the diagram, "defer" means that the change was not approved along with the cut, not that window adjustment itself was permanently rejected. The diagram also does not depict the current entry as an endpoint; it only shows the order of choices made at the time. The problem with the initial draft was that the wording looked as though it had provided an endpoint, while the meeting had actually left a stopping point within the release window.

## The original wording about verifiable material

The meeting materials required: `link the latest reproducible evidence instead of pasting a conclusion`. This sentence was retained not to prescribe wording. It addresses a substitution that was easy to make at the time: a seemingly complete conclusion would appear in the discussion first, followed by an attempt to fill in the call location, platform differences, and maintenance owner. For the wheel cut, this order would make the release window endorse a judgment that had not yet been established.

Another passage stated the approval scope more directly: `Platform changes start from a reproducible call trace and end with an ownership ledger that another maintainer can replay on a different operating system.` This does not mean that every local change must resolve all maintenance issues in one meeting. It means that cross-platform changes cannot consist only of a verbal direction. At minimum, there must be a traceable call chain, along with an ownership record that allows a later maintainer to walk through it again on different operating systems.

These two requirements explain why the review approved only the portions covered by existing material. They do not require pasting a conclusion into the document in place of evidence, nor do they allow "it will be added later" to serve as a reason for expanding the current scope. The initial draft summarized this as "insufficient material," which was too mild; readers could assume that one attachment was missing. What was actually missing was a reasoning chain robust enough to support a coordinated change to the entry and the window.

## What the Windows location could establish at the time

`src/mss/windows.py` and the related call names were the starting point for that discussion. They brought the question of "whether to change the window" back from an abstract opinion to an inspectable location, and enabled the review to conclude that there was no need to replace the facade entry first for this round's cut. That role was real and should be retained.

But this location was never the permanent owner of the window object, much less substitute material for behavior on other operating systems. The initial draft passed over this point in a single paragraph at the end, making it sound as though finding a file on the Windows side had already confirmed the entire platform path. That was not what was done at the time.

More precisely, the location supported a local release decision: the current entry could continue to handle the known scope for this round. It did not automatically answer how the window change would enter in other environments, nor did it confirm which object a future maintainer should follow for further investigation. Turning a location that can begin verification into a global answer was the most common later misreading of this record.

Therefore, any citation of the Windows location here should include its limitation: that path contributed to the decision at the time, but did not replace the cross-platform call chain. This limitation is not a cautious qualification added later; the unresolved question left in the initial draft already shows that the review did not treat it as comprehensive proof at the time.

## What was corrected during the later review

The review found no reason to overturn the conclusion that "the entry and window adjustment would not be combined this round." What needed correction was that the initial draft made the deferral resemble a rejection and made the local location resemble a complete basis.

Regarding the deferral: the second path was not judged to be wrong. It did not enter the wheel cut because the material needed to support that scope was missing at the time. If the call chain and maintenance records are completed later, window adjustment and its relationship to the entry can still be discussed again. This record does not prejudge what that discussion will conclude.

Regarding the local location: `src/mss/windows.py` is not a path name that appeared out of nowhere; it is indeed where the team looked along the call names at the time. But it also cannot be used in place of verification on other platforms. Retaining the path lets readers know that the review was not based only on an abstract preference. Retaining its limitation prevents later readers from treating one location as a complete cross-platform conclusion.

Regarding "the scope covered by existing material": this wording remains in the decision because it was the actual threshold adopted at the time. However, it can easily be misused as a fixed process, as though any subsequent change could be divided across windows in the same way. This record does not extend it in that manner. It describes only how this cut was handled: local material supported local actions, and uncovered portions did not receive automatic approval.

The initial draft also did not answer who should reopen this matter later. That was not a conclusion added after an omission; it was ownership that had not yet been established at the time. The meeting materials called for an ownership ledger, precisely indicating that, without an ownership record, a broader change should not be packaged as completed. Leaving this gap in place is closer to what actually happened than adding a generic handoff statement afterward.

## Opinions that remain open

- If the facade entry is adjusted in the future, first complete a call chain that can be verified across operating systems, rather than merely citing this cut's conclusion.
- If only the window is handled in the future, state whether the action still depends on the current entry; a local window adjustment should not automatically be called an entry migration.
- If an object still has no clear maintenance owner, retaining the entry this round must not be interpreted to mean that no one needs to handle that object anymore.
- The question in the initial draft remains unanswered by this review: whether different operating systems can be verified along the same call chain is still unconfirmed.

These opinions are not new release conditions, nor are they advance approval of a future proposal. They are issues that the wheel cut did not absorb at the time. Removing them would make the old decision appear more complete than it actually was and would allow "retain the current entry" to continue being detached from its original scope.

## Boundary with the subsequent handoff

The maintenance handoff is documented separately in DOC-44. The handoff steps are not repeated here because the wheel cut decision and the handoff record address different questions. The former records why the release scope was not expanded; the latter addresses how maintenance work continues. Having a subsequent handoff does not mean that the material required for coordinating the entry and window has automatically been completed.

This page therefore retains two temporal contexts: the release choice in the initial draft and the tightened wording applied to it after review. It remains a record of an old decision and should not be treated directly as a current architecture guide. The narrowest and most reliable way to cite it is: this round retained the current facade entry, and window adjustment was limited to the scope covered by existing material; the remaining portions were not approved with the wheel cut at the time.

# linux-x11 freeze entry point: code-reading notes

This pass starts at `src/tests/test_gnu_linux.py`. The call names related to linux-x11 in that file are a good starting point: they focus attention on the test location that the GNU/Linux path actually passes through, without inferring a nonexistent relationship from directory names, platform labels, or files with the same name.

```text
src/tests/test_gnu_linux.py
  └─ Call names related to linux-x11
       └─ Direct caller followed in this pass
            └─ First actual consumer of release branch freeze
```

"First" matters here. The goal of this trace is not to list every location that might handle GNU/Linux, but to find the earliest point where freeze actually picks up this call chain. Tracing further would quickly take us into each platform's implementation details. Those details add nothing to the explanation of why this consumer picks up freeze, and would turn a clear entry-point question into a backend walkthrough.

The location of `test_gnu_linux.py` can be misleading at first. It sits in the test directory and reads as though it is the home of linux-x11; in practice, treat it as a place where the call names appear. First confirm the relevant call names in this file, then choose just one direct caller to follow. This is not because the other callers are unimportant, but because this pass is meant to answer where release branch freeze starts being consumed, not to reconstruct the entire capture path.

The cross-platform smoke matrix serves a different purpose in this trace. It helps locate platform combinations: the matrix shows where linux-x11 is included in cross-platform checks, after which we return to the test file and call names. The matrix alone cannot prove which consumer freeze occurs at. It does not replace call edges, and the presence or absence of a platform cell should not change the entry-point judgment.

Follow this sequence during verification to reduce back-and-forth:

1. Get the call names corresponding to linux-x11 from the test file; do not start from similarly named directories.
2. Follow the call name into one direct caller. At this point, confirm only the call relationship, without expanding platform policy into a list of candidates.
3. After that caller, confirm the earliest point where release branch freeze is actually consumed.
4. Look back at the smoke matrix and confirm that it is only cross-check material that helps locate this route.

Files with the same name but no call edge are still worth remembering, but only as signposts. For example, locations whose names contain linux, x11, or cross-platform may explain test coverage on one side, or they may simply be adjacent implementations or historical leftovers. Connecting these files directly into the diagram creates a common misreading: readers assume that matching names mean freeze passes through them. This route includes only the three connected segments; do not add arrows for other matches.

This verification also separated the "test entry point" from the "release consumer." The former helps someone taking over quickly return to the public entry point in the repository; the latter is the actual entry point for release branch freeze. They can be adjacent, but they are not the same thing. If the material shows only smoke results and provides no way back to the call names, return to the test file and keep looking for a direct caller rather than treating a platform entry in the matrix as a consumer.

Keep one stopping point. Beyond the first actual consumer, explaining why a particular display-server branch was selected would enter another maintenance scope. This page does not supply conclusions for that scope. Stopping the route at the consumer is enough to support tracing the freeze entry point. If a platform implementation judgment is needed, record the consumer location reached here and hand it to someone who can answer for that branch.

Do not use that discrepancy in place of this page's call-path judgment.

For anyone starting from the smoke matrix later, the shortest route back is still: return to the call names in linux-x11, find the direct caller confirmed in this pass, and stop at the first actual consumer of release branch freeze. If a path with the same name appears, include it only if it connects back to this chain.

# Display Service Matrix Deviation Postmortem

This page records a deviation during one display-server matrix refresh window. The result planned for the window did not match the result actually visible. The first thing that could be confirmed was that "what was visible did not match what had been scheduled"; this alone could not yet determine whether the refresh had not completed, the result had been overwritten by stale state, or a different state had been retrieved during the check.

## Incident sequence

- When the refresh window reached the check stage, we first found that the visible result did not match the original plan. The discovery point was recorded, but the cause was not written up as a definitive conclusion at the time.
- The first follow-up check searched for entry points using the terms display, server, resource, and instead, and also opened `src/mss/linux.py`. This was only a file location encountered during the investigation at the time, not a permanent ownership confirmed later.
- A temporary recovery was then performed, and the apparent result returned to an acceptable state. The recovery itself did not show that the initial deviation had disappeared, nor that the next refresh would or would not repeat it.
- After recovery, reviewing the records still could not consistently attribute the anomaly to a single step. The initial discovery, temporary recovery, and cause confirmation were kept separate to avoid rewriting the recovery time as the point when the root cause was known.

The resource ownership ledger retained at the time is still useful. It helps cross-check who held which types of resources during the refresh window and at which step the observed result changed, but the table does not provide enough evidence to explain why the visible result diverged from the plan. In particular, the deviation cannot be attributed to the corresponding implementation based only on an entry point or call name.

## Closing the record

The control point later added to this page was: `link the latest reproducible evidence instead of pasting a conclusion`. Specifically: if a deviation of the same kind occurs again, first record a reproducible result, the check location, and the differences before and after recovery, then update the assessment. Do not let "looks normal" after one temporary recovery stand in for what was observed during the anomaly.

This postmortem therefore records impact only within the observed scope: during the matrix refresh, the publicly visible result did not match the plan, and temporary recovery was required. There is no evidence to extend this to failure of all display-server combinations, nor to narrow it to a single-file issue. The original file path and investigation terms are kept here so people who looked into this anomaly at the time can retrace the path; the path itself does not establish the final attribution. At the time, the cause, reproduction conditions, and whether the temporary recovery changed subsequent refresh behavior remained unconfirmed.

# API Review Office Hours Runbook

When an API review office hours message arrives, pause verbal judgment first. Put the CLI version, raw results, and the virtual-display reproducer in this shift's log; if any one is missing, log the issue only—do not turn it into an API conclusion.

On the first line of the handoff, write four things: the public API involved, the platform boundary where the discrepancy appears, the evidence file left behind, and the maintainer who can determine whether this is a contract decision or a local implementation detail. At the first fork where the distinction cannot be made, hand it directly to that maintainer.

If this requires broader permissions, changing public behavior, or setting scope on behalf of the long-term owner, stop immediately and make no commitment to an outcome during office hours.

# Rotation Change Result Troubleshooting Tree

The ticket says incident rotation change is complete, but the same result cannot be verified during handoff. First separate release scheduling from technical acceptance.

```text
Inconsistent results
├─ Can you identify the call entry point and version for windows-gdi?
│  ├─ Yes: Continue comparing the platform call trace using the same input.
│  └─ No: Stop here and fill in the entry point or version first.
└─ Can the traces already be placed side by side?
   ├─ Yes: Check whether the difference occurred before or after the call.
   └─ No: Do not use repeated runs as a vote.
```

Do not assign cause until the entry point, version, and trace are all present.

# Rotation Change Result Troubleshooting Tree

The ticket still says incident rotation change is complete, but the results still cannot be confirmed side by side during actual verification. Treat "complete" only as scheduling status; handle it by separate release scheduling from technical acceptance. First ask for the call entry point and version for windows-gdi, then compare the platform call trace using the same input.

```text
Inconsistent results
├─ Can you identify both the entry point and version for windows-gdi?
│  ├─ Yes: Continue comparing the traces using the same input.
│  └─ No: Stop and fill in the entry point or version first.
├─ Are the two platform call traces comparable?
│  ├─ Yes: Check whether the difference occurred before or after the platform call.
│  └─ No: Stop at the missing trace; do not keep rerunning.
└─ Are they still different after all the materials are complete?
   ├─ Record technical acceptance as undecided; do not put it back into release scheduling.
   └─ Hand over the entry point, version, and both traces; this page ends here.
```

For this pass, confirm only that scheduling status cannot substitute for technical acceptance. Do not record it as a platform difference before side-by-side traces are available.
